title: The Multiplication Rule and Sequential Draws
quickIdea: P(A and B) = P(A|B)P(B): multiply along the path. A chain of conditions gives P(A and B and C) = P(A)P(B|A)P(C|A and B), which is how every without-replacement draw is computed.
remember: The multiplication rule is the definition rearranged, and it holds for dependent events. The independence product P(A)P(B) is the special case P(A|B) = P(A).
Chain rule: multiply the probability of the first event by the conditional probability of each later event given all the earlier ones.
Without replacement the denominator falls by one at each draw, and the numerator falls by one whenever the item drawn was of the kind being counted.
With replacement the fractions repeat, which is exactly the independent case; that is the cleanest way to see why replacement restores independence.
P(A and B) is symmetric, so P(A)P(B|A) and P(B)P(A|B) give the same number. The order of conditioning is free; the answer is not affected.
A question that says 'given that the first ball drawn is red' has already fixed the first draw. Multiplying by 10/25 as well counts the condition twice and is the classic wrong answer 0.3.

example.prompt: A bag holds 10 red and 15 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Find P(both red) and P(second red | first red).
example.work: P(first red) = 10/25. Given a red has gone, 9 red and 15 blue remain in 24 balls, so P(second red | first red) = 9/24 = 0.375. Multiplying: P(both red) = (10/25)(9/24) = 90/600 = 0.15. The conditional question asks only for the second factor.
example.answer: P(both red) = 0.15 and P(second red | first red) = 0.375.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.53 asks for exactly the conditional factor, 9/24 = 0.375, and the wrong answer 0.3 - the unconditional P(both red) - is the mistake the question is built to catch.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.53: a bag contains 10 red and 15 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Given that the first ball drawn is red, the probability (3 decimal places) that both drawn balls are red is ____.
variations.why: After a red is removed, 9 red remain among 24 balls, so the required conditional probability is 9/24 = 0.375. The unconditional P(both red) = 0.15 is a different quantity.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Three cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that all three are aces?
variations.why: Chain rule: (4/52)(3/51)(2/50) = 24/132600 = 1/5525. Each factor is a conditional probability given every earlier draw.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is P(both red) = (10/25)(9/24) but the answer to GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.53 is only 9/24?
variations.answer: Because the question conditions on the first ball being red, so P(first red) is already 1 and drops out of the ratio: P(both red)/P(first red) = 0.15/0.4 = 0.375.
variations.why: The chain rule multiplies the whole path; a conditional question starts halfway down the path.

trap.what: Multiplying the first draw's probability into a question that has already conditioned on the first draw.
trap.why: Conditioning divides by the probability of the condition, and multiplying by it again is the same as not dividing at all - the two cancel in the wrong direction.
trap.counterexample: 0.15 is the probability that both balls are red; 0.375 is the probability that the second is red given the first is. A bag of 10 red and 15 blue gives both numbers, and only one of them answers GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.53.

check.question: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
check.explanation: (3/5)(2/4) = 6/20 = 3/10. The second factor uses the reduced bag of 2 red and 2 blue.
